Bayesian fits with flexyBayes

Source: vignettes/bayesian-fits.Rmd
bayesian-fits.Rmd
library(pollinatoR)

A second engine

pollin_fit() fits with glmmTMB by default. With engine = "flexyBayes" it fits the same model as a Bayesian mixed model, through the flexyBayes package on INLA. Estimates and intervals then come from posterior draws, which carry the uncertainty in the variance components as well as in the fixed effects. The rest of the package takes those draws as it takes the glmmTMB ones: effects, populations, values and guards work unchanged.

In planted-truth simulations the posterior 95% intervals cover close to 95% on designs with unit intercepts and on binomial counts. On designs with a random treatment slope and 12 sites they cover about 91% to 93%. An exact posterior computed by Stan gives the same coverage there, so the shortfall comes from the interval itself with few sites. The package NEWS gives the full results.

This vignette fits one simulated trial on both engines and compares the results: the overall effect, its value, and the effect in each variety.

Installing the engine

Neither package is on CRAN. flexyBayes installs from GitHub, and INLA from its own repository.

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("AAGI-AUS/flexyBayes")
install.packages(
  "INLA",
  repos = c(getOption("repos"), INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"),
  dependencies = TRUE
)

The engine is checked when a fit is made. Without both packages, engine = "flexyBayes" stops with a message naming the one that is missing.

A simulated trial

Eight canola varieties are grown in six blocks. In every block each variety has bagged plants, closed to insects, and open plants. The response is the number of pods per plant. Varieties differ in how much they gain from insect visits: each has its own treatment effect on the log scale, drawn around a mean of 0.4.

set.seed(2026)
varieties <- sprintf("V%d", 1:8)
blocks <- sprintf("B%d", 1:6)
trial <- expand.grid(
  plant = 1:3,
  trt = c("Bagged", "Open"),
  block = blocks,
  variety = varieties,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
block_effect <- setNames(rnorm(6, 0, 0.2), blocks)
variety_effect <- setNames(rnorm(8, 0, 0.2), varieties)
variety_slope <- setNames(rnorm(8, 0.4, 0.25), varieties)
log_mu <- 3 + block_effect[trial$block] + variety_effect[trial$variety] +
  variety_slope[trial$variety] * (trial$trt == "Open")
trial$pods <- rnbinom(nrow(trial), mu = exp(log_mu), size = 15)
nrow(trial)
#> [1] 288

pd <- pollin_data(trial, response = "pods", treatment = "trt", unit = "block")
ds <- pollin_design(pd, arms = c(excluded = "Bagged", open = "Open"), layout = "rcbd")
est <- pollin_estimand(ds, "dependence", "ratio", "loss")

The planted loss share of each variety is 1 - exp(-slope):

planted <- 1 - exp(-variety_slope)
round(planted, 2)
#>    V1    V2    V3    V4    V5    V6    V7    V8 
#> -0.27  0.52  0.43  0.37  0.18  0.44  0.27  0.30

The same model on both engines

The fixed part and the random terms are the same on both engines: the treatment as a fixed effect and a random intercept per block. A negative binomial family is set explicitly, so both engines use it.

# One INLA fit per model instead of the best of three.
options(flexyBayes.inla_best_of = 1L, flexyBayes.silence_default_prior_note = TRUE)
fit_tmb <- pollin_fit(est, family = glmmTMB::nbinom2())
fit_fb <- pollin_fit(est, engine = "flexyBayes", family = glmmTMB::nbinom2())
fit_fb
#> <pollin_fit>
#>   engine    : flexyBayes 
#>   family    : dependence 
#>   contrast  : Open vs Bagged 
#>   model     : <response> ~ trt + block 
#>   pods      : nbinom2, 288 rows

pollin_effects() reads the loss share from each fit. On glmmTMB the interval is the delta interval, taken over the fixed and random effects jointly. On flexyBayes it is the posterior interval: the estimate is the median of the posterior draws of the loss share, the interval their equal-tailed 95% interval, and p.value is NA.

eff_tmb <- pollin_effects(fit_tmb)
eff_tmb$table[, c("estimate", "std.error", "conf.low", "conf.high", "interval")]
#>    estimate  std.error  conf.low conf.high interval
#> 1 0.3289669 0.03075109 0.2659063 0.3866105    delta
eff_fb <- pollin_effects(fit_fb, n_draws = 1000L, seed = 1L)
rbind(eff_tmb$table, eff_fb$table)[
  , c("estimate", "std.error", "conf.low", "conf.high", "interval")
]
#>    estimate  std.error  conf.low conf.high  interval
#> 1 0.3289669 0.03075109 0.2659063 0.3866105     delta
#> 2 0.3272635 0.03177408 0.2624175 0.3864073 posterior

With a few hundred plants and a block intercept as the only random term, the two engines agree closely. Both intervals carry the uncertainty in the block variance: the posterior integrates over it, and the delta interval approximates it through the joint precision of the Laplace approximation.

From posterior draws to a value

On a flexyBayes fit, pollin_draws() uses method = "posterior", its only method there. Each draw takes the fixed effects, the block effects and the variance parameters jointly from the posterior, and the two arm means are recomputed from them. A seed sets both R’s random number generator and INLA’s, so the draws repeat exactly.

dr_fb <- pollin_draws(fit_fb, n = 1000L, method = "posterior", seed = 1L)
dr_fb
#> <pollin_draws>
#>   family   : dependence (E2) 
#>   scale    : ratio 
#>   basis    : loss 
#>   estimate : 1 - Bagged/Open (loss share) 
#>   response : pods 
#>   method   : joint posterior draws (INLA) 
#>   engine   : flexyBayes 
#>   draws    : 1000 
#>   columns  : overall

The draws go into pollin_value() exactly as simulation draws do. The market inputs below are illustrative.

canola <- pollin_market(
  quantity = 3600,
  price = 700,
  unit = "t",
  currency = "AUD",
  year = 2025,
  source = "Illustrative inputs",
  crop = "canola"
)
dr_tmb <- pollin_draws(fit_tmb, n = 1000L, seed = 1L)
rbind(
  summary(pollin_value(dr_tmb, canola, channel = "dependence")),
  summary(pollin_value(dr_fb, canola, channel = "dependence"))
)[, c("median", "conf.low", "conf.high", "currency", "method")]
#>     median conf.low conf.high currency     method
#> 1 824536.6 662938.5  977626.5      AUD simulation
#> 2 824704.1 661292.0  973746.4      AUD  posterior

The vignette From dependence to value covers the channels, populations and the double-count guard. Each of them takes posterior draws.

The effect in each variety

The varieties were planted with different loss shares. There are two ways to estimate them.

The unpooled way fits a separate treatment effect for each variety, as a fixed interaction, with pollin_fit(by = "variety"), and reads them with pollin_effects(). Each variety’s estimate uses only that variety’s plants.

fit_by <- pollin_fit(est, family = glmmTMB::nbinom2(), by = "variety")
unpooled <- pollin_effects(fit_by)$table

The pooled way gives the varieties a random intercept and a random treatment slope, with pollin_fit(pooled = "variety"), and reads the effect at each level with pollin_cate(). A variety whose estimate is uncertain, or far from the rest, is pulled towards the overall effect. A slope on a unit column, such as site in a multi-site study, is declared in the design with pollin_design(slope = ) instead.

fit_pool_tmb <- pollin_fit(est, family = glmmTMB::nbinom2(), pooled = "variety")
cate_tmb <- pollin_cate(fit_pool_tmb, n = 1000L, seed = 1L)
fit_pool_fb <- pollin_fit(
  est,
  engine = "flexyBayes",
  family = glmmTMB::nbinom2(),
  pooled = "variety"
)
cate_fb <- pollin_cate(fit_pool_fb, n = 1000L, seed = 1L)
cate_fb
#> <pollin_cate>
#>   by       : variety 
#>   scale    : ratio 
#>   basis    : loss 
#>   estimate : 1 - Bagged/Open (loss share) 
#>   interval : 95% posterior, equal-tailed (1000 draws) 
#> Pooled: partial pooling through the random treatment slope on variety 
#>  response       contrast level    estimate  std.error    conf.low conf.high
#>      pods Open vs Bagged    V1 -0.03765513 0.12818008 -0.32705765 0.1824290
#>      pods Open vs Bagged    V2  0.52106684 0.04963124  0.42457435 0.6117453
#>      pods Open vs Bagged    V3  0.41298387 0.05809948  0.28693099 0.5161875
#>      pods Open vs Bagged    V4  0.30969114 0.06842357  0.17060470 0.4301068
#>      pods Open vs Bagged    V5  0.15062658 0.09294636 -0.05052131 0.3107053
#>      pods Open vs Bagged    V6  0.28531109 0.06768565  0.13552124 0.3989924
#>      pods Open vs Bagged    V7  0.41258595 0.06276025  0.27923342 0.5295937
#>      pods Open vs Bagged    V8  0.26678756 0.07837561  0.09901543 0.4024860
#>  pooled  n     family scale basis distribution  interval
#>    TRUE 36 dependence ratio  loss      nbinom2 posterior
#>    TRUE 36 dependence ratio  loss      nbinom2 posterior
#>    TRUE 36 dependence ratio  loss      nbinom2 posterior
#>    TRUE 36 dependence ratio  loss      nbinom2 posterior
#>    TRUE 36 dependence ratio  loss      nbinom2 posterior
#>    TRUE 36 dependence ratio  loss      nbinom2 posterior
#>    TRUE 36 dependence ratio  loss      nbinom2 posterior
#>    TRUE 36 dependence ratio  loss      nbinom2 posterior
#> Unpooled: not carried by this fit, which pools variety; the fixed per-level contrasts come from `pollin_fit(by = "variety")` without the slope, read with pollin_effects().

The print keeps the two kinds apart: the table holds the pooled contrasts, and a line points to the unpooled ones. Set side by side with the planted values:

compare <- data.frame(
  variety = varieties,
  planted = round(planted, 2),
  unpooled = round(unpooled$estimate, 2),
  pooled_glmmTMB = round(cate_tmb$table$estimate, 2)
)
compare
#>    variety planted unpooled pooled_glmmTMB
#> V1      V1   -0.27    -0.14          -0.10
#> V2      V2    0.52     0.55           0.49
#> V3      V3    0.43     0.43           0.45
#> V4      V4    0.37     0.31           0.33
#> V5      V5    0.18     0.12           0.17
#> V6      V6    0.44     0.28           0.33
#> V7      V7    0.27     0.43           0.37
#> V8      V8    0.30     0.26           0.26
compare$pooled_flexyBayes <- round(cate_fb$table$estimate, 2)
compare
#>    variety planted unpooled pooled_glmmTMB pooled_flexyBayes
#> V1      V1   -0.27    -0.14          -0.10             -0.04
#> V2      V2    0.52     0.55           0.49              0.52
#> V3      V3    0.43     0.43           0.45              0.41
#> V4      V4    0.37     0.31           0.33              0.31
#> V5      V5    0.18     0.12           0.17              0.15
#> V6      V6    0.44     0.28           0.33              0.29
#> V7      V7    0.27     0.43           0.37              0.41
#> V8      V8    0.30     0.26           0.26              0.27

Pooling pulls the extreme varieties inwards: V1 rises on both engines, and V2 and V7 fall. This does not bring every variety closer to its planted value. V1 was planted with a negative loss share and moves away from it, while V7 moves towards it. Partial pooling lowers the error over the varieties as a whole, not for each one.

The two engines differ in how they get the interval. On flexyBayes it comes from the posterior draws, as for the overall effect. On glmmTMB it is approximate: the fixed effects and the varieties’ slopes are drawn jointly from a normal distribution with the covariance of the delta interval, so the draws carry the correlation between them.

cate_tmb$table[, c("level", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
#>   level   estimate    conf.low conf.high
#> 1    V1 -0.0997176 -0.36423304 0.1181613
#> 2    V2  0.4878510  0.37137752 0.5770984
#> 3    V3  0.4502143  0.33706411 0.5386251
#> 4    V4  0.3255154  0.20910660 0.4358281
#> 5    V5  0.1719329 -0.01475916 0.3131227
#> 6    V6  0.3327006  0.20124754 0.4425291
#> 7    V7  0.3687068  0.23003453 0.4841452
#> 8    V8  0.2630115  0.11233377 0.3785739

In this trial pooling narrows the intervals of most varieties on both engines, though not all of them.

When glmmTMB estimates the slope variance at zero, every variety’s pooled effect equals the overall one, and the conditional variances carry no information. pollin_cate() stops on such a fit rather than report intervals; the unpooled contrasts or the flexyBayes engine remain.

What the engine refuses

The flexyBayes engine refuses, by name, what it cannot fit faithfully.

flexyBayes can also fit with brms, but the posterior draws of a brms fit are not part of version 1 of the flexyBayes extension API, which is what pollinatoR reads. The brms backend is refused:

try(pollin_fit(est, engine = "flexyBayes", backend = "brms"))
#> Error : The flexyBayes engine fits on INLA only: posterior draws of a brms fit are not in the flexyBayes extension API version 1.

Five families are mapped to their flexyBayes counterparts on INLA: nbinom2() (as negative_binomial), poisson(), binomial(), Gamma(link = "log") (as gamma) and beta_family() (as beta), each with its log or logit link. Any other family, such as Tweedie, is refused:

try(pollin_fit(est, engine = "flexyBayes", family = glmmTMB::tweedie()))
#> Error : Family 'tweedie' of 'pods' has no flexyBayes counterpart on INLA. The flexyBayes engine fits nbinom2, poisson, binomial, Gamma, beta; choose one with `family =`, or use `engine = "glmmTMB"`.

flexyBayes on INLA does not fit a correlated random treatment slope, the unstructured slope that glmmTMB fits as (trt | variety). The flexyBayes route fits a variety intercept plus an independent effect for each variety-by-arm cell instead. That is a restricted form of the unstructured slope: the variance is the same in both arms and the correlation between arms cannot be negative. The pooled effects on the two engines therefore come from slightly different models, and where the true arms vary unequally between varieties they can disagree for that reason alone.

Priors

Priors are passed to flexyBayes::flexybayes() through ... as written, in the flexyBayes prior language of flexyBayes::fb_prior(). pollinatoR adds no priors of its own. Without one, flexyBayes uses its default, a half-normal prior on each random-effect standard deviation and a nearly flat prior on the fixed effects. Here the treatment coefficient, the log of the open-to-bagged ratio, gets a normal prior with standard deviation 1:

fit_prior <- pollin_fit(
  est,
  engine = "flexyBayes",
  family = glmmTMB::nbinom2(),
  prior = flexyBayes::fb_prior(b("trtOpen") ~ normal(mean = 0, sd = 1))
)
pollin_effects(fit_prior, n_draws = 1000L, seed = 1L)$table[
  , c("estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")
]
#>    estimate  conf.low conf.high
#> 1 0.3267644 0.2618674 0.3858719

flexyBayes::prior_summary() on a fitted model, fit_prior$fits$pods, lists each prior and the INLA parameter it reached.
